pages.title: PREDICT
pages.text: The $(item)Propagation Predictor$() says which HF bands should be open to a place over the next 24 in-game hours: a band by hour grid like the real VOACAP's.$(br2)Tab picks the target: $(thing)coordinates$() (X and Z), a $(thing)callsign$() (a player online, or an APRS station this computer heard; F5 lists them), or a $(thing)distance and bearing$() (4000 90 is 4000 blocks east). Enter predicts.

It works out each hour with the same sums your radios use: the band's line of sight and its $(l:radiocraft:propagation/bands)skip ranges$() by day or night, the band's $(l:radiocraft:propagation/solar_weather)condition$() in the solar weather, and the noise floor. It reads the sky as the $(l:radiocraft:computer/solar_weather)Solar Weather$() program does: an Ionospheric Processor, or a radio with a real antenna.

pages.title: Reading the grid
pages.text: $(2)G$() good, $(e)F$() fair, $(c)P$() poor (data and CW get through, voice hardly), - closed. $(3)c$(): closed to voice but open to CW, which carries half as far again. $(thing)L$() means line of sight (ground wave): no sky needed.$(br2)The top rows give the clock hour, ** for day and .. for night. Below the grid: the best band now and each band's best hour.

The current solar event is known until it ends, and the next one once the forecast has it. Past that the predictor guesses the sky stays as it is: those hours are dimmed, in lower case.$(br2)It assumes a dipole at each end at full power, and leaves out hills and your real antennas, so treat it as a guide. F6 prints the grid, F7 saves it as PREDICT.TXT. It refreshes every 20 seconds.
A blank floppy and a clock.
